\begin{abstract}
Self-consistency yields large gains on discrete-answer tasks, but named entity recognition (NER) produces \textit{sets} of entities with partial overlap, where no majority vote analog exists.
We evaluate five confidence signals---four instance-level (structural and surface agreement) and one per-sample (log-probability)---for quality estimation and sample selection on three NER benchmarks spanning a difficulty gradient (SciERC, CoNLL, WNUT-17), using 4B--8B models.
All signals achieve reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45, AUROC up to 0.82), supporting selective prediction and error flagging.
However, quality estimation does not translate to sample selection---the \textit{correlation-selection gap}: best-of-$N$ selection approximately matches greedy decoding ($T{=}0$) despite 13--18~pp oracle headroom.
We diagnose two mechanisms: (a)~\textit{instance degeneracy}---fine-tuned models produce identical outputs for 21--58\% of instances, eliminating selection headroom despite positive within-instance utility--F1 correlation (median $\rho{=}0.52$); and (b)~\textit{log-probability compression}---median within-instance range of 0.041 nats, with entity-token isolation revealing intrinsic overconfidence rather than format-token dilution.
A five-layer ablation chain and a LoRA-rank ablation (degeneracy 7\% vs.\ 21\%) confirm these mechanisms are intrinsic to capable fine-tuned models: reducing degeneracy is necessary but not sufficient for selection.
Closing the gap likely requires learned per-sample scoring.
\end{abstract}

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We evaluate five confidence signals for quality estimation and sample selection in LLM-based NER, revealing the \textit{correlation-selection gap}: moderate quality estimation ($\rho{=}0.38$ on medium-difficulty NER, up to 0.45 on a ceiling-effect control) coexists with selection that approximately matches greedy decoding ($T{=}0$) without significantly outperforming it.
The gap stems from two mechanisms: instance degeneracy (21--58\% of instances produce identical F1 across all $N$ samples, scaling with model capability and eliminating selection headroom despite positive within-instance utility correlation) and LP compression (the only per-sample signal has median within-instance range of 0.041 nats).
Diagnostic ablations---free-form decoding, entity-token LP isolation---confirm compression is intrinsic rather than an artifact of constrained decoding or format-token dilution.
The gap is demonstrated in the medium-difficulty regime where models achieve moderate but imperfect accuracy; signal rankings shift with difficulty and collapse at the capability boundary in the small-model regime (3B--8B).
Whether these mechanisms persist at 70B+ scales is an open question; trained verifiers and an exploratory extension to relation extraction (Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}) are promising directions.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We evaluate five confidence signals for quality estimation and sample selection in LLM-based NER.
Structural and surface agreement signals reliably predict output quality ($\rho$ up to 0.45, AUROC up to 0.82), supporting selective prediction and error flagging regardless of selection regime.
However, quality estimation does not translate to sample selection---the \textit{correlation-selection gap}: selection approximately matches greedy decoding ($T{=}0$) despite 13--18~pp oracle headroom.
The gap stems from two jointly operating mechanisms: instance degeneracy (21--58\% of instances produce identical F1 across all $N$ samples, scaling with model capability) and LP compression (median within-instance range of 0.041 nats).
A LoRA-rank ablation reduces degeneracy from 21\% to 7\% without enabling selection, confirming that low degeneracy is necessary but not sufficient; diagnostic ablations confirm both mechanisms are intrinsic to capable fine-tuned models rather than artifacts of constrained decoding.
Signal rankings shift with task difficulty and collapse at the capability boundary in the 3B--8B range tested; whether these mechanisms persist at 70B+ scales is an open question.
Closing the gap likely requires learned per-sample scoring \cite{cobbe2021verifiers}; an exploratory extension to relation extraction (Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}) is a promising direction.

\paragraph{Best-of-$N$ with learned verifiers.}
\citet{gao2023scaling} establish scaling laws for best-of-$N$ selection with learned reward models, showing that BoN performance scales log-linearly with $N$ but eventually degrades due to reward overoptimization.
Our unsupervised signals face a more fundamental limitation: they cannot rank candidates at all (instance-level signals) or rank them too weakly (LP compression), making the overoptimization regime irrelevant.
Trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, lightman2024verify} and quality-aware decoding \cite{fernandes2022quality} learn per-sample scoring that may bridge this gap; our LoRA-rank ablation (degeneracy 7\% vs.\ 21\%, selection still fails) suggests that verifier training is necessary beyond merely increasing output diversity.
Fine-tuning itself contributes to the problem: \citet{kirk2024understanding} document diversity collapse in RLHF-trained models; our instance degeneracy is an analogous phenomenon in supervised fine-tuning, where stronger models converge to more uniform outputs.
Nucleus sampling \cite{holtzman2020curious} improves diversity in open-ended generation, but our constrained structured outputs limit the diversity that temperature scaling alone can recover.
